Elias placed the phone inside the cup holder rather than returning it to the mount.
“Why did you help me?” Zoe asked.
Answers based on instinct sounded false when spoken aloud.
Because she had checked the child lock before entering the car.
Because Mac had called her family while giving Elias no family contact.
Because the woman at Arrivals had handed Zoe across a bureaucratic line and vanished.
Because Cain’s people expected every ordinary person to prefer safety over interference.
Because his trainee had once stood where he was told not to stand and made a choice Elias had spent years trying to reduce to a mistake.
He gave Zoe the part that belonged to her.
“Because Cain does not get to take another child if I can stop him.”
It did not fully reach either of them.
Zoe looked towards the side window.
“I think you understood the flight before I did. I think you knew the collection route had been exposed. I think you tried to steal a car because every other route belonged to someone else.”
“I also think you have told me only what you needed me to know.”
Zoe looked down at the backpack.
The movement confirmed more than words would have.
Elias kept his eyes on the road.
“Mac thinks you are his niece,” he said.
The sentence altered the structure of the job.
Elias looked at her in the mirror.
Zoe had already withdrawn behind the backpack.
“Mac sent me into an airport to collect a child under a false relationship. Cain’s people followed us and called me by a name I buried. Questions are now part of the journey.”
“I agreed not to interrogate you in Arrivals.”
“That depends on what I know before then.”
Zoe’s fingers moved along the repaired edge of one backpack strap.
At the airport, she had held it as a shield.
At the restaurant, as an anchor.
Now she positioned it on her lap and looked at the zip.
He watched the road and allowed the decision to happen without observation becoming pressure.
“There’s something in the bag,” she said.
“Because you nearly drove my car down a ramp rather than let me near it.”
Zoe traced one finger along the zip but did not open it.
Elias’s hands tightened around the wheel.
She looked at him through the mirror.
Elias did not ask the third question.
“Because you gave me the answer you intended to give.”
The road ahead divided around a construction zone.
Elias selected the lane with two exits available rather than one.
A temporary speed limit reduced traffic around them.
Zoe said, “The bag is why they followed me.”
“I believe Cain’s people ignored a public restaurant, offered me a clean exit and risked exposure because recovering you mattered more than remaining invisible. The bag may explain why.”
“You locked it when we left the restaurant.”
“You could still open it from inside.”
“You didn’t tell the server I was lying.”
The final words tightened the air.
He corrected the claim rather than defending it.
“I will not call him without telling you first.”
“Even if you think it’s a safety problem?”
“If it becomes immediate, I act. Otherwise, I tell you.”
The light across the cabin darkened and returned.
Zoe asked, “Where are we going now?”
Elias looked at the navigation screen.
The grandmother’s address remained west, five hours away after the deliberate detour.
The phone had become a compromised object.
The hatchback might already be known.
The road still belonged to Mac’s instruction until Elias chose otherwise.
“For the moment, we keep moving,” he said.
Her hands closed around the backpack.
She could start with the decoy.
That was the shortest explanation for the flight.
It was also the wrong beginning.
The decoy had existed because of everything that came before it.
Starting with the decoy would turn the story into a failed escape plan.
It would conceal what had made escape necessary.
Zoe looked out at the motorway.
Fields moved past beyond the barrier.
The previous Tuesday, she had known the names of roads near school, which teachers assigned homework on Tuesdays and where Helen kept spare batteries in the kitchen drawer.
Now an ocean sat between that life and the old hatchback.
He did not prompt her again.
“You can’t interrupt every time you think something doesn’t make sense.”
Elias looked at her in the mirror.
The number settled into the car.
He reduced speed as traffic thickened ahead.
The first day returned in pieces.
A van where no van belonged.
Helen’s voice from the kitchen earlier that morning.
Jackie finishing a sentence Zoe had not needed to complete.
The ordinary life before anyone admitted it had been temporary.
“It started on an ordinary Tuesday,” Zoe said. “That’s the part people would get wrong afterwards. I hadn’t run away. I hadn’t arranged to meet anyone. I was just walking home.”
He had learned that much already. Zoe came forward at her own pace. Pushing only sent her back into silence.
“I was still in my school uniform,” she said. “Helen had asked me to get milk.”
That morning, Helen had called up the stairs three times before Zoe answered.
Zoe had appeared at the top of the stairs with one shoe on, her tie hanging loose and her hair only half tied back.
Helen stood below holding a travel mug in one hand and Zoe’s lunch in the other.
“I know where the other one is.”
Zoe looked back towards her bedroom.
It had been that kind of morning.
Nothing dramatic. Nothing that felt important enough to remember.

Brian had already left for work. The radio was on in the kitchen. Helen had burnt one piece of toast and scraped the black edge over the sink before spreading jam across what remained. Zoe ate it standing up while trying to fasten her tie.
At school, Jackie took one look at her and said, “You forgot—”
“I was going to say your dignity.”
Jackie grinned and handed over the book Zoe had lent her the week before.

They spent lunch sitting on the low wall behind the sports hall, sharing a packet of crisps and arguing about whether the substitute maths teacher wore the same shirt every day or owned five identical ones.
The final bell went at half past three. Jackie walked with Zoe as far as the crossing where their routes separated.
“Message me when you get home,” Jackie said.
Zoe watched her reach the opposite pavement before turning towards home.
By five, the school day had already become ordinary enough to forget.
Helen was in the kitchen, opening cupboards with increasing irritation.
Helen looked into the fridge as though the milk might have concealed itself behind the vegetables.
Zoe was still wearing most of her uniform. She had thrown her blazer over a chair and changed her shoes, but the white shirt, dark skirt and black tights remained. She took the money Helen held out.
Helen sighed and added a pound coin to her palm.
Helen said it lightly. The kind of warning adults gave because they believed saying it counted as protection.
Zoe rolled her eyes and left.
The corner shop was exactly where it had always been.

The same faded advertisements covered the window. The same bell gave the same tired jangle above the door. The man behind the counter was watching football on a small television beneath the cigarettes and barely looked up when Zoe placed a bottle of milk and a chocolate bar in front of him.
Outside, the evening was warm enough that she put her earphones in and carried her blazer folded over one arm.

She had walked them so often that her body knew the route without instruction: left at the boarded-up florist, across beside the post box, past the garden with the stone dog, then straight until her front door came into view.
Nothing about the street had changed.
A van pulled alongside her before she registered that it was slowing.
White. No company name. Dirt around the rear wheel arch.
A hand closed over her mouth before she could produce more than a muffled gasp. Another arm locked around her waist and lifted her backwards.
The bottle struck the pavement and split.
Milk ran white along the kerb.
That was the last thing she saw of the street before someone pulled her into the dark.
She had no chance to fight. By the time her body understood what was happening, the door had slammed shut and the van was already moving.
A man told her to stay quiet.
Zoe kicked once and struck metal. Pain travelled up her heel. The grip on her wrists tightened until her fingers went numb.

Because she needed to breathe, and because the van was turning hard enough to throw her against the side, and because there were at least two people inside with her and she could not see either of their faces properly.
The air inside smelled of diesel, damp fabric and something sweet that had spilled into the floor mat.
She listened for traffic. Tried to judge speed. Tried to remember how long they travelled.
Fear kept breaking the count apart.
“You hadn’t been contacted beforehand,” Elias said.
It was not phrased as an accusation.
Zoe looked at him through the mirror.
She looked towards the side window.
“I stayed awake,” she said. “The whole way.”
“Not enough to find it from the route. Enough to know they didn’t take me far.”
“Traffic. The roads. We stopped twice, but not for long. And when they opened the door again, it was still light.”
The van stopped inside a garage.
She knew because the sound changed first. The engine noise came back from close walls. Then a metal door rattled down behind them, shutting out the street before the side door opened.
The men walked her through an internal door into a house.
They did not think she needed one.

The house sat on a quiet residential road with a trimmed lawn and a child’s bicycle lying on its side in the front garden. Zoe saw it through the narrow window beside the front door as they passed. One wheel turned slightly in the breeze.
The curtains were drawn in every room she could see, upstairs and down.
Inside smelled of carpet cleaner and something colder underneath it that she could not name.
They walked her through the front hall.
A locked glass cabinet stood against one wall. Rows of folders filled the shelves inside, each labelled with a number instead of a name.
Nobody tried to block her view.
The cabinet was locked. The adults had already decided that meant whatever it contained was safe from her.
Further along, a study door stood open by several inches. Zoe saw a safe set into the wall, its keypad glowing faint green, before one of the men reached across and pulled the door shut.
A woman met them in the kitchen.
Mid-thirties. Pleasant face. Hair tied back. The kind of ordinary that made the room feel less safe rather than more.
She poured Zoe a glass of water she had not requested and placed it on the table as though this were a normal visit to a normal house.
“You’ll be processed tomorrow,” the woman said, in the same tone she might have used for
She smiled briefly—the way adults smiled at children they had already decided not to explain anything to—then told one of the men to take Zoe upstairs.
The bedroom contained a single bed, a wardrobe and a window too high for her to reach without standing on something.
The window opened no more than an inch.
The lock was on the outside of the door.
Zoe checked all three before she sat on the bed.
She lay in a room that was not hers and listened to footsteps pass in the corridor. Pipes clicked inside the wall. A door opened somewhere below and closed again.
Whenever she shut her eyes, she saw the bottle striking the pavement.
She wondered whether Helen had gone looking for her yet.
Whether Jackie had sent the message she had promised to send.
Whether anyone had found the chocolate bar crushed beside the broken bottle.
had ever meant anything good for anyone.
Elias took the next junction more slowly than necessary, letting the silence remain hers.
Elias merged back into the traffic.
He checked the mirror once. Not because Mac had asked him to collect her. Not because the job required it.
“Keep going when you’re ready,” he said. “I’m listening.”
Zoe nodded and, after a moment, continued.
They passed a sign for services, but Elias continued beyond the junction. Zoe had not asked to stop, and for the first time since the airport, he did not think she needed to.
“What did they want from you?” he asked.
Zoe did not answer straight away. She watched a lorry overtake them, slow and heavy, before she spoke.
“At first I didn’t know,” she said. “I just knew there were rules.”
She woke in a different room from the one she had been locked in the first night.
It was smaller. Bars had been fitted inside the window frame and painted the same white as the wall, easy to miss at a glance. Someone had left clothes folded at the end of the bed.
A woman Zoe had not seen before entered without knocking and recited the rules in the even, unhurried voice of someone who had said them many times.
Don’t look the buyers in the eye.
Zoe asked what a buyer was.
The woman studied her for several seconds. Her expression did not change, but something in it made the question feel like another rule Zoe had already broken.
Later, Zoe was taken downstairs to a room with too many chairs.
Six children sat inside. She counted them immediately, though she suspected there were others elsewhere in the house. None looked directly at anyone else.
She understood, without being told, that this was another rule.
A girl no older than ten flinched when a man passed too close.
He crouched beside her and said something too quietly for Zoe to hear. The girl went rigid, staring at one point on the floor until he stood and walked away.
Zoe watched, made herself very small and said nothing.
It was in that room, on the second afternoon, that she first heard the name.
Two of the older children whispered near the wall.
The whispering stopped the moment an adult’s shadow crossed the doorway, but Zoe had already caught fragments.
She turned the name over privately for the rest of the day.
Nobody whispered it as though it belonged to someone who could be reasoned with.
“Was that the only time?” Elias asked. “Someone punished for a small thing?”
Her voice had flattened again. Elias had noticed it before: whenever she described something instead of allowing herself to feel it, the words became precise and distant.
“It happened a lot,” she said. “It wasn’t really about the rule. It was to remind everyone the rules existed.”
Elias kept his eyes on the road.
“That’s not discipline,” he said. “That’s a demonstration.”
Zoe glanced at him in the mirror.
“Because I’ve seen people run rooms like that before.”
Later that afternoon, a man arrived.

Every conversation stopped before he reached the doorway. One of the adults stepped aside without being asked. The woman who had given Zoe the rules straightened so quickly that the movement looked rehearsed.
He did not look at any of the children.
He walked through to a study at the back of the house. The woman followed him inside and pulled the door closed.
A few minutes later, she came back out carrying a water jug.
She turned and went back into the study. The door did not quite latch behind her. As Zoe passed, she heard Cain speaking inside.
A pause followed. Paper moved against paper.
“Filed under the original number. Nothing’s changed.”
Zoe did not understand the words.
She understood the change in their voices.
Both had become quieter. More careful. Each sentence placed as precisely as a foot on uncertain ground.
She was still near the doorway when it opened.
The woman almost walked into her.
“Water,” Zoe said, raising the empty jug.
The woman’s gaze remained on her for one beat too long.
She stepped out carrying a folder. Then a phone began vibrating in her pocket.
She placed the folder on the kitchen counter before answering the call and moving several steps away.
A number had been written on the tab instead of a name.
The woman did not close it. She did not turn it over. She did not appear to consider that Zoe might understand anything she saw.
A photograph lay on top of the papers.
A young girl, perhaps six or seven, with her hair in two plaits. She had been caught laughing at something outside the frame.
Zoe stared at the picture while the jug filled.
The face felt familiar before she understood why.
A photograph she did not remember anyone taking.
The tap continued running until water reached the rim and spilled across her fingers.
The woman was still speaking quietly into the phone.
Zoe left the jug on the counter and returned to the room with too many chairs.
She knew the folder concerned her. She knew the adults had kept a photograph of her for years. She knew there was a number connected to her that existed before she understood any of this.
She did not yet know what the number meant.
She did not know who the buyer was.
She did not know why somebody had been keeping records on her since she was a small child.
But she knew she had not been taken at random.
Elias let the silence settle after that part.
In the mirror, Zoe was watching him. He kept his face still, although the muscle in his jaw tightened once before he made it stop.
“You knew the folder was about you,” he said.
“No. I didn’t know what the number meant, why the picture was years old or how long they’d been keeping records on me.”
“I knew who everyone in that house was afraid of.”
“When did you understand what they were preparing you for?”
Zoe’s fingers found the strap of the backpack in her lap.
“Not all at once,” she said. “That night, they stopped letting me sleep.”
“By Friday morning, I hadn’t slept properly for three nights,” Zoe said. “The first night was me. After that, they made sure.”
Elias’s hands tightened slightly on the wheel, then relaxed.
He let the silence remain until Zoe chose to fill it.
The first night, fear kept her awake.

Every sound beyond the locked door became footsteps approaching. Every movement of the pipes became someone touching the handle. When she closed her eyes, she saw the bottle breaking against the pavement and milk spreading along the kerb.
By morning, she had slept in fragments so short they felt imagined.

Wednesday passed in rules, rooms and faces she did not yet know how to read. By evening, exhaustion had begun to settle into her limbs. She thought that might help. She thought eventually the body would take what it needed whether the mind agreed or not.
That was when the interruptions began.
The light remained on above the bed.
When Zoe started to drift, the door opened.

Sometimes a woman came in to ask whether she wanted water. Sometimes a man told her to sit up while he checked the window latch, though nobody had touched it. Once they moved her to another room for less than an hour, then returned her to the first without explanation.
Each time, whatever edge of sleep she had reached disappeared.
The questions were ordinary enough to sound harmless.
What did Helen cook most often?
Had anyone ever taken her abroad?
They repeated questions she had already answered, changing one word at a time.
When Zoe pointed that out, the woman smiled.
Zoe stopped answering unless she had to.
A television played somewhere downstairs, always loud enough to reach her and never clear enough to understand. Part of her mind kept reaching for sentences that never finished.
By Thursday morning, time had begun to come loose.

Meals arrived, but she could not always tell whether they belonged to breakfast or lunch. She remembered the colour of the plate more clearly than what had been on it. She counted the woman’s footsteps from the door to the bed three separate times and got three different answers.
She did not understand the design then.
She only knew that every interruption made the next question harder to hold onto. After enough hours, even anger required concentration.
So she began choosing what to keep.
The sound of the back door.
Which floorboard outside the room clicked beneath adult weight.
The smell of cigarette smoke that appeared before the tall lieutenant did.
She could lose an hour and still remember a lock.
“What were they trying to get you to agree to?” Elias asked.
“I didn’t know yet,” Zoe said. “Not exactly.”
She adjusted the backpack against her knees.
“I knew something was coming. You could tell by the way the house changed.”
“People moved faster. Doors that were normally closed stayed open. Clothes appeared on beds. The woman with the rules kept checking the same list.”
“One of the men tested the lock on the study twice,” Zoe continued. “Nobody had tried to open it. He checked anyway.”
“And they hadn’t told you what it was.”
“They didn’t think I needed to know.”
Thursday afternoon blurred at the edges, but certain details remained sharp.
Fresh clothes arrived in transparent bags.
The children were separated by age and moved between rooms. One woman inspected fingernails. Another checked hair, skin and teeth without explaining why.
Zoe held the older photograph in her memory: her own face at six or seven, laughing at something outside the frame. The file. The number. The word buyer spoken behind a door.
Each detail seemed separate because the adults had kept them separate.
That evening, the tall lieutenant entered the room.
The smell of cigarette smoke reached Zoe before he did.

He stood in the doorway without speaking, watching the children as though he were checking condition rather than seeing people. His gaze travelled from face to face, pausing longest on the ones who shifted or looked down.
When his eyes reached Zoe, they remained there.
She recognised him now as the man she would later see at the service station—the one whose face had emptied when he recognised Elias.
At the time, he was simply the person everyone else adjusted around.
Zoe did not look away first.
Exhaustion had stripped away the smaller fears. Only the thing they were preparing her for remained.
On Thursday night—the third night without proper sleep—Zoe heard two women talking in the corridor.
Their voices were low and businesslike. They discussed the following morning as though it were a scheduling problem.
“Depends if she’s settled by morning. He doesn’t like them jumpy.”
“She’ll be fine. They always are by the time we’re done.”
Zoe lay beneath the unbroken light and kept her breathing even.
She refused to guess what tomorrow meant.
Every possibility her mind produced was worse than the one before it.
Later, when the corridor had gone quiet again, one of the older girls was brought into the room.
Zoe recognised her as one of the children who had whispered Cain’s name near the wall.
The girl sat on the floor beside Zoe’s bed as though she had been told to wait there. She kept her eyes on the opposite wall.
After several minutes, she leaned just close enough to speak without turning her head.
“Don’t eat anything they give you before it,” the girl whispered. “Don’t drink anything either, if you can help it.”
The girl’s fingers tightened around the hem of her sleeve.
The girl’s face changed by less than a movement.
A door opened somewhere along the corridor.
The girl stood immediately and moved away before anyone entered.
Zoe held the warning in her mind for the rest of the night, testing it against everything she had seen.
They had offered water she had not requested.
They monitored what the children ate.
They always were by the time the adults were done.
Zoe began to understand what she was to them.
Made presentable for someone waiting on the other side of a word she still did not fully understand.
They had taken almost every decision from her.
The older girl’s warning gave one decision back.
That did not make it unimportant.
Zoe decided she would not eat.
And whatever happened in the morning, she would make them believe she had.
Elias drew a slow breath through his nose and held it before speaking.
“You don’t have to finish this part now.”
“You don’t owe me the rest because you started.”
The answer came quickly enough that he believed her.
Zoe looked down at her hands.
“I’ve been carrying it alone,” she said. “It’s heavier than the talking is.”
Elias looked at her in the mirror and did not ask again whether she was sure.
Zoe nodded and, after a breath of her own, continued.
Zoe’s hand found the strap of her backpack again.

It had been happening for most of the drive: fingers closing around the webbing, tightening, loosening, then returning as though the bag might disappear if she stopped checking it was there. Elias had noticed the first time. By the fourth, he had learned not to mention it.
“Day four,” she said, “is why I still have this. And why I’m here at all, instead of still in that house.”
She pulled the backpack closer to her stomach.
They came for her early, before she had time to become afraid in any organised way.

The older woman entered carrying a small plastic tray. She was different from the one who had recited the rules. Brisker. More carefully dressed. Her hair was pinned back so tightly that it seemed to pull the expression from her face.
On the tray sat a paper cup and a folded square of white cloth.
“Drink this,” she said. “It’ll help you relax before the showing.”
The word landed with all the others Zoe had collected over the previous three days: buyer, original number, prepared, showing. Words everyone else understood and nobody would explain.
She thought of the older girl’s mouth barely moving beneath the unbroken light.
Don’t eat anything they give you before it. Don’t drink anything either, if you can help it.
Her hand shook. She let it. Nobody expected a frightened child to have steady hands.
The liquid smelled faintly of orange with something medicinal underneath. She lifted it to her lips, tipped her head back and allowed

enough into her mouth to wet her tongue. Bitterness spread immediately. She held the rest against the inside of her cheek, trapped behind her back teeth, while the woman watched the bottom of the cup rise.
Then she lowered the empty cup.
The woman took it and used the white cloth to wipe a drop from Zoe’s chin, not gently or cruelly, but with the impersonal care of someone cleaning a mark from glass.

Zoe crossed to the sink, bent low and spat the liquid into the basin. She turned on the tap and rinsed the orange trace away before it could settle. Then she scooped water into her mouth, swilled once and spat again.
The bitterness remained behind her teeth.
There was no way to know how much she had swallowed by accident.

She looked at herself in the small mirror above the basin. Her face looked pale and detached, her eyes too bright within it. She let her mouth hang open. Let her shoulders sag. Tried to make her gaze slide past her own reflection rather than meet it.
The first version looked like acting.
By the fourth, she looked vacant enough to frighten herself.
When the lock turned again, she was sitting on the edge of the bed with her hands loose between her knees.
Two women entered. One carried a comb. The other carried Zoe’s school uniform on a hanger.
For a moment, seeing it was worse than seeing unfamiliar clothes would have been.

Her white shirt had been washed and pressed. The blazer was brushed clean. Even the tie had been retied into a neat knot and loosened just enough to pass over her head. The uniform looked ready for an ordinary Friday morning, as though it had been waiting patiently for her to finish whatever interruption had kept her from school.
“Stand up,” one of the women said.

They changed her without asking her to help. The shirt was buttoned to the throat. Her tie was straightened. One woman brushed her hair while the other inspected her face, lifting her chin towards the light and turning it first one way, then the other.
A thumb pressed beneath Zoe’s eye, testing the skin there.
They spoke over her and around her, never to her except to issue instructions.
The woman with the comb caught a knot and pulled hard enough to bring water into Zoe’s eyes.
Zoe let her focus drift towards the wall.
She was learning that people saw what they expected to see.
A sedated child did not glare.
A sedated child did not calculate distances.
A sedated child did not notice that one woman wore a ring of keys at her left hip and the other checked the corridor before opening the door.
So Zoe noticed everything and made it look like nothing.
He kept his eyes on the road. When he spoke again, his voice had lost some of its earlier distance.
“Some of it got into me.” Zoe rubbed her tongue against the back of her teeth as though the taste might still be there. “Not enough to put me out. Enough to make everything feel half a second late.”
Elias accepted that with a small movement of his head.
“Because I didn’t know what was coming,” she said. “And not knowing was worse when I couldn’t think.”
They took her downstairs by a route she had not used before.

The house changed as they moved through it. The rooms where the children slept and waited had cheap paint, bare bulbs and furniture chosen to survive damage. This part had carpet thick enough to swallow footsteps. Framed prints hung on the walls. A vase of artificial white flowers stood on a table beneath a mirror, the sort of arrangement that might have belonged in a private clinic or an expensive solicitor’s office.
Nothing in it admitted what the house was.
The showing room was colder than the corridor.

Bright panels had been fitted into the ceiling, too white and too even. One wall was covered from skirting board to ceiling by darkened glass, too perfect and too black to belong in an ordinary room. A square of pale tape marked a position on the carpet. A single chair stood against the far wall, beyond reach of the taped box.
The brisk woman guided Zoe into the square.
The woman adjusted the fall of her blazer, tugged one sleeve down and lifted Zoe’s chin with two fingers.
Zoe looked at the darkened glass.

It returned a schoolgirl in a clean uniform: small, pale, exhausted, her hair brushed smooth. No locked doors. No barred window. No children in the room with too many chairs. Nothing to explain why she stood beneath lights while unseen adults decided something about her.
A faint click came from behind the glass.
Then a man’s voice, softened by a speaker hidden somewhere above her.
Only briefly, but Zoe felt it.
“The original record is held on site.”
A third voice, a woman this time, said, “Medical history?”
The questions continued in the same calm register.
Whether she had been placed before.
Whether the number had been used across borders.

The words did not form a whole picture for Zoe, but the tone did. They were inspecting her the way Brian inspected a second-hand car before buying it: not because he cared how it felt, but because he wanted to know what problems came with it.
The room tilted a fraction to the left. The small amount of liquid she had swallowed seemed to move behind her eyes. She concentrated on the lower edge of the glass, where it met the skirting board.
There was a tiny chip near the corner.
A flaw no one had bothered to repair.
A voice behind the glass said, “Have her turn.”
The woman placed a hand on Zoe’s shoulder and rotated her.
Zoe let her feet drag. Let her head follow too late. She made herself into what they thought they had made her.
The woman pressed Zoe’s chin down and told her to open. A light passed briefly across her teeth.
There was movement behind the glass.
Then the first man’s voice again, no longer quite so calm.
“This number doesn’t match the transfer sheet.”
The brisk woman’s fingers tightened once on Zoe’s shoulder.
A different man answered from farther away, not through the speaker.
“The transfer number is current. The original record carries the first identifier.”
A door opened somewhere behind the glass. Footsteps moved into the corridor outside. The woman beside Zoe looked towards the sound, then back at the glass.
Zoe was already standing exactly where they had placed her.
Then voices rose deeper in the house.
“You don’t get access to the archive.”
“I get access to the record I paid to verify.”
A heavy impact shook something in the adjoining room. Another voice cut in, sharper, ordering both men to stop. Furniture scraped. A door slammed. Glass broke with a hard, bright crack.
The speaker above Zoe hissed and went dead.
She remained inside the taped square.
Her heart beat so violently that the edges of her vision pulsed with it.
If someone remained behind it, they saw a drugged girl waiting where she had been told.
The corridor beyond the open door was empty.
“I was scared the glass still had someone behind it.”
“It didn’t feel good. It felt like standing there while the only chance I might ever get disappeared.”
“Waiting and freezing aren’t the same thing.”
Zoe looked at him in the mirror.
Elias took a moment before answering.
“Because one has an end you choose.”
Zoe stepped out of the square.
Her right foot landed badly. The floor seemed to shift beneath it and she caught the doorframe before she fell. The drug had not made her helpless, but it had not left her untouched either.
The shouting continued somewhere towards the front of the house. A man swore. Someone else shouted for security.
Two doors down, the archive stood open.
Someone had brought the original folder out in a hurry and never pulled the door closed behind them.
Zoe had seen the room only in fragments before: a green keypad light, the edge of a safe, numbered folders lined with unnatural precision. Now the door was wide enough to show all of it.

Hard drives filled its shelves, arranged upright in black cases like a row of teeth. Numbered folders sat in stacks beneath them. An old leather ledger lay closed on the desk, thick enough to stop a door. Beside it, a laptop displayed a pale screen crowded with boxes and codes Zoe could not read.
A cable ran from the laptop to a small black drive.
The screen showed the same number the adults had argued about in the showing room.
And beside the drive lay an open folder.
A girl of six or seven, hair in two plaits, laughing at something beyond the edge of the picture.
She had seen the photograph two days earlier on the kitchen counter and recognised herself then. Now, with the folder open and the number exposed on the tab, she understood why it mattered.
The folder had been brought out for the showing. The argument had been about the number written across it.
Zoe crossed the room and took it.

Beside the open folder lay a clear plastic property bag containing the possessions taken from her on the first night: exercise books, a pencil case, a crushed packet of tissues and her backpack, one strap twisted beneath it. A white label on the bag carried the same number as the folder.
The backpack smelled faintly of rain and the lavender detergent Helen used at home.

She did not know what was on the attached drive. She knew only that adults had checked it while discussing her records, that the original file and the number had changed the buyers’ voices, and that the argument had emptied the showing room and pulled everyone towards the archive.
Whatever was on the drive mattered enough to make them forget her for a few seconds.

Zoe shoved the drive into the backpack, closed the zip and moved behind the archive door just as a man passed the opening. She saw only the side of his dark jacket and one bloodied hand held close to his chest. He did not look into the room. He was calling for someone, voice ragged with anger, moving towards the showing room.
Zoe waited until his footsteps faded.
Then she ran the other way.
The corridor ended at a narrow service passage.
Cold air touched her face before she saw its source.
At the far end, an exterior door stood open. A wooden crate held it back while two men struggled to move an injured man towards a waiting
vehicle beyond it. One shouted for someone to clear the way. The other looked down at the blood on his hands.
A woman’s voice sounded behind her.
For one terrible second, the backpack caught on the handle.
She pulled hard enough to wrench her shoulder, tore the strap free and stumbled outside.

The house stood on a quiet residential street lined with clipped hedges and broad driveways. A delivery van was parked opposite. Somewhere nearby, a lawnmower droned. Curtains moved in an upstairs window and settled again.
Nothing looked like escape because nothing looked like captivity.
She had no idea which direction led home.

At the end of the street she turned left, then right, then left again, trying to make it harder for anyone behind her to see where she had gone. The backpack struck her spine with every step. Her school shoes slipped on damp pavement. Twice she looked back and saw no one.
The third time she nearly ran into a parked car.
Her legs had forgotten what running was for.

After several streets, she ducked behind a row of commercial bins and crouched there, fighting for breath, one hand clamped over her mouth. A car passed slowly. She pressed herself against the brick wall until it moved on.
She stayed until she could count ten breaths without losing the number.

The neighbourhood gave way to a busier road: petrol station, pharmacy, takeaway, traffic lights. The signs meant nothing to her, but buses did. A stop stood beside the pharmacy with a route map scratched beneath its plastic cover.
Most of the place names were unfamiliar.
She had been there with Helen. School trips changed buses there. From the interchange she could find a route she knew.
The electronic display said twelve minutes.
The wait felt longer than anything since the van door had closed.
When the bus arrived, Zoe stepped aboard and stopped beside the driver.
The driver glanced at her uniform, then at the queue behind her.
“Go on,” he said, already looking past her to the next passenger.
No adult seeing through the clean blazer to the numbered folder and stolen drive pressed against her back.
Zoe moved down the aisle and sat where she could see the front door reflected in the window.

For the first five minutes she was certain the house would appear around every corner. Then she was certain someone would board at every stop. A man in a dark coat climbed on and her whole body locked before he turned towards an empty seat without looking at her.
Outside, ordinary life continued with an almost insulting calm.
Two boys in another school’s uniform shoved each other and laughed.
A woman argued into her phone beside a pushchair.
Traffic waited, moved and waited again.
Nobody knew where Zoe had been.

At the town-centre interchange, she stepped down into noise, diesel fumes and a crowd thick enough to hide inside. Electronic boards clicked through destinations. She found a route number she recognised from trips with Helen and stood among a cluster of schoolchildren waiting beneath it.
For the first time since the van door had closed, she looked like every other child around her.
She kept both arms around the backpack.
Her second bus was almost full. She stood for three stops with both arms still wrapped around it, then took a seat when one became free.
Familiar streets began to appear in fragments: the supermarket with the broken letter in its sign, the park where Brian complained about dog owners, the junction before her school.
She could have got off there.
For a moment she imagined walking through the school gates, finding a teacher, saying everything at once before anyone could stop her.
Then she remembered the folder in her bag.
The number instead of her name.
Adults in the house talking about documents, transfers and placements as though every official thing she knew could belong to them too.
Home was where frightened children were supposed to go.

By the time she reached her stop, afternoon had thinned towards evening. The sky above the houses was turning the colour of old metal. Her legs shook when she stood, and the driver watched her in the mirror, perhaps wondering if she was ill, perhaps not wondering anything at all.
Zoe stepped down and walked the final streets.
She knew every crack in the pavement.
The house with the wind chimes.
The corner where Jackie sometimes waited for her in the mornings, pretending she had arrived by accident.
Helen always turned it off before evening to save electricity.
The house looked exactly as it had four days earlier. Curtains half-drawn. Brian’s car in the drive. A plant pot Helen kept meaning to replace leaning beside the step.
She walked to the door and stood before it with one hand raised.
She had passed through that doorway thousands of times without once thinking about what it meant to be allowed back inside.
Elias’s eyes moved briefly to the backpack in her lap.
“You knew the folder was yours,” he said.
“I knew the photograph was me. I knew the number was the same one they’d been arguing about. I didn’t understand the rest until later.”

“I didn’t know what was on it.” Zoe’s fingers tightened around the strap again. “I still don’t. Not properly. But it was connected to the computer when they checked my records. They cared enough about the archive to start fighting over who could see it. I thought—”
“I thought it might tell me who I was.”
Elias looked back to the road.
The motorway noise filled the car: tyres, wind through the narrow gap at the top of his window, the distant complaint of a lorry changing gear behind them.
“I kept both. I never opened the drive. I opened the folder the night before the flight.”
Elias’s hands rested lightly on the wheel, but the stillness in them had changed.
“Keeping them was a decision,” he said.
“Most decisions don’t feel like decisions while you’re making them. You recognised the gap. You took your own file. You took the thing they were protecting. You carried both out.”
“You can be scared and still choose.”
Zoe looked at him properly then.
Her grip on the strap loosened by a fraction.
“I never thought of it that way.”
“Most people don’t,” Elias said. “Doesn’t make it less true.”
The silence that followed was different from the ones before it.
Not empty. Not demanding. Just shared. “There’s more,” Zoe said after a while. “I know.” Elias kept his eyes on the road. “Take your time.”
“Day five,” Zoe said, “started the night before. When I knocked on my own front door.”
Elias glanced at her in the mirror, then back to the motorway.
A lorry behind them indicated for several seconds before moving into the slow lane. The ticking reached them faintly through the glass, regular and patient, until the vehicle dropped away.
“I thought getting home would fix everything,” Zoe said. “That was the part I didn’t understand. Not how wrong I was. Why.”
Elias did not tell her that children were supposed to believe in home. He did not tell her that the belief was reasonable, or that losing it was not her fault.
None of them would have changed what happened when the door opened.

Helen always turned it off before evening had properly settled, because leaving it burning when nobody needed it was, in her words, the same as feeding coins into the wall. Zoe had heard the complaint so often she could repeat the exact sigh that came before it.
Now the light shone over the step and the leaning plant pot Helen had been promising to replace since spring.
The door opened before she could do it a second time.
Helen stood there in slippers and the blue cardigan she wore when the house was cold. For one second she simply stared. Her face seemed unable to decide what expression belonged on it.
Then she made a sound that was not quite Zoe’s name and pulled her inside.

Zoe knew that because Helen held too tightly and because her breath broke against Zoe’s hair. She smelled of lavender detergent, hand cream and the onions she had been chopping for dinner. Familiar smells. Safe smells. The kind Zoe had tried to remember in the locked bedroom when the television would not stop talking through the wall.
Helen felt it and tightened her grip.
For a few seconds Zoe let herself believe she had reached the end of it.

Her hands moved over Zoe’s face, her shoulders, the sleeves of the cleaned uniform, checking without quite knowing what she was checking for. Relief remained in her expression, but something else had entered it.
Her eyes moved past Zoe towards the street.
He did not come forward. He looked over Zoe’s head, first towards the gate, then the parked cars, then the dark hedge along the neighbour’s drive.
“Did anyone see you come in?” he asked.
He stepped outside far enough to look both ways along the road. The porch light fell across his face. Zoe could see the small muscle near his
temple moving while he counted windows, cars, people who were not there.
Helen drew Zoe farther into the hallway. Brian closed the door, turned the lock, fitted the chain and then checked the lock again.
He checked doors twice before bed, pressed the car key twice after parking and always went back to make sure the cooker was off, even when Helen had used it.
Until that night Zoe had thought it was simply one of the things that made him Brian.
He reached past her and switched off the porch light.
That was the first thing that made it feel wrong.

Her school photograph still stood on the narrow table beneath the mirror, one corner hidden behind a bowl full of keys. A pencil mark inside the cupboard door recorded the year she had grown three inches and Brian had accused the tape measure of lying. Helen’s ceramic hedgehog sat on the windowsill, the one Zoe had made when she was seven and which looked nothing like a hedgehog unless somebody explained it first.
Her shoes were still beneath the radiator where she had kicked them off four days earlier.
Helen led her into the kitchen and sat her at the table. The smell of onions had begun to catch in the pan. Helen turned off the hob without looking at it.
The question came so late Zoe nearly did not recognise it for what it was.

Helen crouched in front of her. There were tears drying on her face now, but she kept pushing Zoe’s hair back from her forehead as if the right arrangement of it might make the last four days less real.
The unfinished question hung between them.
Zoe looked down at her hands.
Brian had gone to the front window. He moved the curtain aside by the width of two fingers, looked out, let it fall, then checked the back door.
“We should call the police,” Helen said.
“That she’s home. That she was taken.”
“And when they ask where she came from? When they ask for papers? Names? Dates?”
“I know how long she’s been missing.”
Brian’s face changed, not into anger exactly, but into the expression he wore when a bill arrived that he had been expecting and still could not afford.

Mac was the man she had always been taught to call Uncle Mac. He sent birthday money through Helen and telephoned at Christmas from whichever city he happened to be in. There were photographs of him, but never many, and never the kind where everybody stood close enough to touch.
He belonged to the family story in the way distant relatives often did: accepted because adults had always spoken as though there was nothing to question.
“Not yet. She needs a doctor. She needs sleep.”
Something in Brian’s voice ended the argument.
Zoe had heard him use that voice with delivery drivers and once with a man who reversed into their garden wall. She had never heard him use it with Helen.
He took his phone from his pocket and left the kitchen.
Then she looked at the backpack still looped around Zoe’s shoulders.
Zoe’s hands closed around the straps.
The answer had come out harder than Zoe intended. For a moment they both seemed surprised by it.
“It’s only your school things,” Helen said gently.
Helen’s gaze moved over Zoe’s face. Whatever she saw there made her lower her hands.
That small surrender frightened Zoe almost as much as Brian checking the street.
Helen made toast because it was the only food Zoe could keep down. She cut it diagonally, the way she had when Zoe was small, and spread too much butter near the edges.
The scrape of Helen’s knife against the plate made her think of the metal spoon touching the glass of sedative. A car door closed outside and her whole body went rigid before she could stop it.
He crossed to the front window again.
“It’s next door,” he said after checking. “Just next door.”
He sounded irritated, but not with her.
Helen brought a bowl of warm water and cleaned the scrape along Zoe’s wrist. Her touch was careful. She murmured apologies whenever Zoe flinched, though she had not caused the injury.

For a while she was simply Helen again: the woman who sat beside Zoe through fevers, who saved wrapping paper if it had not torn, who could identify which cupboard door had been left open from another room.
Then Brian returned with the phone in his hand.
Helen’s fingers stopped around the cloth.
“He said nobody was to call anyone until he got here.”
Zoe looked from one of them to the other.
Brian put the phone face down on the table.
“You can’t go near the windows,” he said. “You can’t call school. You can’t call Jackie. No messages, no social media, nothing that tells anyone you’re here.”
“Because the people who took you may be looking for you.”
It was the first answer that sounded like protection.
Zoe wanted to accept it. She wanted so badly to accept it that for several seconds she almost did.
Then she remembered Brian’s first question at the door.
Brian picked up the phone again.
“How does he know what this is?”
Zoe recoiled before she could stop herself.
Helen removed her hand as though burned.
Her bedroom was exactly as she had left it.

The duvet was turned back from the morning she disappeared. A school jumper lay over the chair. Glow-in-the-dark stars still clung to the ceiling, though most had lost their light years ago. On the shelf above her desk stood a row of photographs: Zoe and Helen on a beach, Brian holding a collapsed tent pole while Zoe laughed, Jackie pulling a face behind a birthday cake.
There was so much proof that she belonged there that the room seemed to be trying too hard.
The old lock was meant for privacy, not security. Brian could open it with a coin. Still, the click helped.
She took off the backpack and placed it on the bed.
For several minutes she only looked at it.
The folder was inside. So was the black drive. Two objects from a room that should not have existed, resting among exercise books and a pencil case with a broken zip.

Not in that room. Not with Helen moving downstairs and Brian speaking in low bursts into his phone. Not while some part of her still believed that whatever was written inside might destroy the only version of home she had left.

She closed the backpack and pushed it beneath the bed, behind a plastic storage box filled with old school projects. The ceramic mask she had made at nine stared up from the box through a sheet of tissue paper, one eye larger than the other.
Then Zoe sat on the floor with her back against the bed.
From downstairs came the sound of cupboards opening, the kettle filling and Brian checking the front door for the third time.
She had imagined home as the place where she would finally be allowed to stop watching.
Instead, everybody else had started watching too.
That night she woke three times.
The first time, she thought the television from the trafficking house was playing beyond the wall.
The second, she heard footsteps on the landing and crawled silently from the bed before recognising Helen’s soft slippers.
The third time, voices carried through the heating vent.
Helen and Brian were in the kitchen. They spoke carefully, believing the closed doors and running boiler would hide them.
“We can’t keep her here if they know she’s back.”
“Where else is she supposed to go?”
Then Brian, quieter: “That’s not how they see it.”
Zoe pulled the duvet closer around herself.
Helen said something she could not hear.
Brian answered, “The money won’t matter if this comes out. None of it will.”
“When, then? When the police ask why there was no proper adoption? When they ask who arranged it?”
Helen’s voice dropped so low that Zoe caught only pieces.
Brian made a sound with no humour in it.
Zoe stared into the darkness until the stars above her bed slowly appeared, faint green points holding their shape long after they should have stopped glowing.
Mac arrived before nine the next morning.
He came alone in a dark car that looked recently washed. Brian opened the door before he knocked.
Zoe heard his voice from the landing.
Calm. Ordinary. The voice of a man asking whether a delivery had arrived on time.
Helen and Brian became quiet around it.
Zoe sat at the top of the stairs with her knees pulled to her chest and watched through the banister.
Mac removed his coat and handed it to nobody. He folded it once over his arm before entering the living room.

He was not physically imposing, and nothing about him demanded attention. His suit was dark without being expensive enough to notice, his hair neat, his face the kind a person could pass in a corridor and fail to remember ten seconds later.
Even seated in Helen’s living room, he seemed designed to leave no strong impression behind.
For an instant his gaze met Zoe’s through the wooden rails.
It was a relative’s smile. Practised, restrained and entirely wrong for the room.
“There you are,” he said. “Come down, Zoe. We need to talk.”
Mac did not repeat himself. He simply waited.
Eventually Zoe stood and descended, keeping one hand against the wall because the floor still moved unexpectedly beneath her.
Mac’s gaze touched the hand she kept against the wall and moved on.
They sat in the living room. Helen took the armchair beside Zoe. Brian remained standing until Mac looked at him, then sat as well.
Mac placed both hands on one knee.
Helen’s eyes were red from the night before.
Zoe felt the folder beneath the bed as clearly as if it were still pressed against her spine.
Mac studied her for a moment.
He did not accuse her of lying. He moved to the next question.
“Did you speak to anyone after you left?”
“What did you tell him?” Mac asked.
“Nothing. He let me on because I was in uniform.”
For the first time, something like approval crossed his face.
The word made Zoe feel ill.
Mac turned to Helen and Brian.
“No police. No social services. No hospital unless I arrange it. What have you told the school?”
“Keep it that way. Nobody tells them she has returned. Nobody outside this house learns she is here.”
Helen gripped the arm of her chair.
“The people who took her know the people she knows. That is precisely the problem.”
His tone did not change. He spoke as though explaining a simple mistake in a timetable.
A pause, brief enough that Helen and Brian might not have noticed it.
Mac smiled again, but less of it reached his eyes this time.
Brian said her name in warning.
Mac raised one finger without looking at him.
“You have had a terrible experience,” Mac said. “You are exhausted, frightened and surrounded by information you do not yet understand. I am trying to keep you alive long enough for that to change.”
Every word could have been true.
Zoe still did not believe him.
“Why do they listen to you?” she asked.
The conversation was over because he had decided it was.
At the doorway he turned back to Zoe.
“Do not contact your friend Jackie. Not for any reason.”
Zoe’s face gave her away before she could stop it.
“This is not punishment,” he said. “It is protection.”
Helen cried in the kitchen after Mac drove away.
Not loudly. Helen had always cried as though apologising for the inconvenience of it, wiping each tear before the next one could fall.
Brian stood beside her with one hand on her shoulder.
“Hold it together,” he said. The words were firm, but his thumb moved once across the fabric of her cardigan. “Just until this is done. Then we can fall apart.”
For a moment none of them moved.
The hurt on Helen’s face was immediate and genuine.
“Why didn’t you call the police when I disappeared?”
“We called Mac when you didn’t come home.”
“We did what we could without making it worse.”
The question seemed to empty the kitchen.
Helen sat down at the table and covered her face.
Nobody asked Zoe what had happened inside the house. Not properly. They asked whether she had been seen, whether she had spoken, whether she had brought attention back with her.
They measured danger by how close it had come to their door.
That was when Zoe first understood that protection and management could use the same locks, the same lowered voices and the same order to stay inside.
From the outside they could look identical.
From within, only one of them cared what happened to the person behind the door.
Elias kept his hands light on the wheel.
Anger would have been easier. What settled in him was colder and more deliberate.
Zoe looked at him in the mirror.

“I think she loved me,” Zoe said. “I think Brian did too, in whatever way he knew how. That’s the part that makes it worse. If none of it was real, I could throw the whole thing away. But some of it was. I just don’t know which parts.”
Elias drove for several seconds before speaking.
“You may never get one clean answer.”
“That doesn’t mean you imagined the good parts.”
The motorway barrier flashed silver beside them, post after post, each one appearing and vanishing before it could be studied.
“Mac told me not to contact Jackie,” Zoe said eventually. “That made me think about something she’d told me before.”
Her voice had changed. Softer now, carrying the shape of somebody remembered before the memory became dangerous.
“She collected stories. Rumours, things adults said when they forgot children were listening. I never knew where she got half of them, and she liked not telling me. Made her feel mysterious.”
A small smile appeared and disappeared.
“There was one she said people in Mac’s world still talked about years later. Like a ghost story, except nobody believed in the ghost until they had to.”
Elias’s eyes remained on the road.

“Two crews were starting a war,” Zoe continued. “Fighting over territory that used to belong to Mac before either crew existed. Somebody sent a watcher in. Just gather intelligence. Watch, listen, report back. Don’t interfere.”
The traffic ahead slowed. Elias eased off the accelerator earlier than necessary.
“Then both crews decided the watcher belonged to the other side. They came for him on the same night, from different directions. Jackie said they thought they were killing each other’s advantage.”
Zoe watched the back of Elias’s head.

“She said the watcher was the only one who walked out. Every person from both crews was gone. And afterwards, the watcher never reported back. No body. No confirmation. Just disappeared with everybody else left behind him.”
The movement was smooth, but he checked the empty mirror twice.
“Jackie knew the date,” Zoe said. “She said people remembered it even if they never said why.”
For less than a second, the engine note softened.
His voice was level enough to sound rehearsed.
Elias kept his gaze on the grey road ahead.
Not towards the mirror this time. Towards Elias himself.
Roadworks had reduced four lanes to two, bringing the traffic to a standstill beneath a row of red gantry signals.
“Jackie came to the house on Sunday,” she said. “That was when we made the plan. And when I put her where they could reach her.”
Elias eased the car forward with it.
Jackie arrived at twenty past ten on Sunday morning with a supermarket bag in one hand and two phones in the other.
One was hers. The second was an old pay-as-you-go handset with a charger looped around it.
Helen opened the front door only as far as the chain allowed.
“Jackie, please. This is not a good time.”
“It hasn’t been a good time since Tuesday.”
Jackie followed the movement with her eyes, then looked back at her.

“I’ve called Zoe thirty-seven times. I’ve messaged her on everything except the calculator app. School says family emergency. Brian says she’s away. You say nothing. So either she’s in there, or something’s happened and nobody thinks I deserve to know which.”
Jackie planted one trainer against the step before Helen could close the door.

She was smaller than Helen and half her weight, but years of holding doors open with a hip while carrying shopping, washing or a sleeping child had made her difficult to move once she decided where she belonged.
“That she doesn’t want to see me.”
Zoe had been standing halfway down the stairs, listening.
She came into the hallway before Helen could answer.
For a moment, all the sharpness went out of her.
The supermarket bag slipped against her leg. Her mouth opened, but no sound came.

Zoe had expected questions. She had expected Jackie to cross the hall and touch her face, or demand to know where she had been, or begin talking too fast in the way she did when fear had nowhere else to go.
Instead Jackie said, very quietly, “Purple penguin.”
It was nonsense to anyone else.

During their first month as friends, they had invented a way to prove it was really them online. One used the challenge phrase. The other had to answer with the deliberately incorrect response they had fixed years earlier.
Helen looked between them, then removed the chain.
Jackie crossed the hallway and wrapped both arms around Zoe.
She did not squeeze too hard. She did not ask whether Zoe was all right when the answer was visible.
“One hour,” Helen said. “Then you leave. You don’t call anyone, you don’t post anything, and you do not tell anyone Zoe is here.”
Jackie looked over Zoe’s shoulder at her.
“Because the people who took her may still be looking.”
The fear in them lasted less than a second before she put it somewhere else.

Not only sweets or crisps, though there were both buried near the bottom of the bag. She had brought bread rolls, sliced cheese, two apples, a packet of biscuits, bottled water and a small container of pasta she had made the night before.
“You look like you’ve been living on air,” she said when they reached Zoe’s room.
She locked the door, tested the handle, then pushed the desk chair beneath it even though the chair would not have stopped anybody determined enough to enter.
Zoe watched her divide the food without thinking: one roll for now, one wrapped for later; water opened first; apple kept until Zoe had eaten something heavier.
Jackie had been arranging meals for people since before either of them understood that children were not supposed to be responsible for feeding whole households.
Her mother had died when she was six.

At first Jackie had done only what a six-year-old could do. Cereal poured into bowls. A bottle warmed too long. Her four-year-old sister’s hair dragged into an uneven ponytail. The baby changed with so much talcum powder that the room looked as though it had snowed.
Then her father’s drinking grew worse, and the jobs grew with it.

Laundry. School lunches. PE kits. Permission slips. Dinners made from whatever remained in the cupboard. Keeping two sisters and a little brother quiet when their father came home angry, then waking them early enough to hide what had happened before school.
By the time Jackie was ten, she could run a house better than most adults.
Then the children had been taken.
Jackie had been sent to one placement, her sisters to two others and her brother somewhere nobody would name. She had not seen any of them since.
She spoke about them rarely. When she did, she used the present tense.
My brother sleeps with one foot outside the blanket.

Zoe had understood early that this was one of the rules of loving Jackie: the missing were not to be treated as dead simply because the adults responsible for them found disappearance more convenient.
Jackie placed the pasta container in Zoe’s lap.
The joke was ordinary enough that Zoe almost cried.
Jackie saw it coming and looked away, pretending to inspect the shelf above the desk.
“Your ceramic mask still looks haunted,” she said.
Zoe laughed once. The sound came out wrong, but it came.
For the first time since the van door had closed, she was with somebody who did not need her to explain who she had been before it happened.

The locked bedroom came before the van. The older girl came before Cain. The showing broke apart halfway through because Zoe could not describe the room and remain inside her own body at the same time.
Jackie never told her to slow down.
How many doors between the bedroom and the stairs?
Had anyone used Zoe’s name before she gave it?
Did Cain’s people know about Helen and Brian?
Had Zoe seen the same men more than once?
The questions did not feel like interrogation. Jackie had always listened by building a place for the answer to stand.
When Zoe mentioned the archive, Jackie looked towards the bed.
“You keep checking under there,” she said. “Not like you’re scared something’s hiding. Like you’re scared it isn’t.”
Zoe pulled the backpack from behind the storage box.
She did not remove the folder or the drive. She opened the zip just far enough for Jackie to see the edge of the file and the black casing beneath it.
“What if it explains one thing and gives you twenty worse questions?”
Jackie did not reach for it.

Helen had tried to take it. Mac had never asked what Zoe had brought back. Jackie was the first person who understood that the fact Zoe possessed something did not make it available to everyone who claimed to care about her.
Zoe told her about the grandmother.

About the flight Mac was arranging. About the person who would collect her at the other end. About the address she had never seen and the relative nobody had mentioned until the day Mac needed somewhere to send her.
Jackie sat back against the bed.
“I don’t know what real means anymore.”
“Mac chose all of it. The flight, the person meeting me, the house.”
“And the people who took you know him.”
“You do the thing with your left eyebrow when you’re leaving out the worst part.”
Then, as they had done hundreds of times in classrooms, bedrooms and message threads long after midnight, they reached the same conclusion without either needing to finish the sentence.
“We need them to believe another route,” Jackie corrected.
The plan began on the back of an old science worksheet.
The curtains had remained closed since she came home.
“Phones,” Jackie said. “Accounts. Searches, if they’re good.”
“I think people who steal children probably don’t rely on luck.”
She wrote SEE above the first box, FIND above the second and BELIEVE above the third.

This was how Jackie had survived her father. How she had got three smaller children washed and dressed before school after nights when no adult in the house could stand. She broke impossible things into jobs small enough to do.
By midday they had the shape of it.
The false route would lead away from the airport.

A late coach to the coast. An overnight crossing. A train beyond the port. Enough ordinary detail to survive a quick check and enough uncertainty to look like a plan made by frightened people in a hurry.
They assumed Zoe’s old accounts might be watched, but using the house network could alert Helen, Brian or Mac. Jackie switched off the Wi-Fi on her phone and used mobile data instead.
Zoe logged into an old shared account they had once used for homework files.
She sent a message from herself to a second account they both knew:
Plan changed. Coach tonight. Same place we talked about. Don’t reply.

They saved a route map in the shared cloud folder, added a screenshot of the coach timetable and created a draft note containing the ferry terminal, the departure time and a partial booking reference.
They opened the booking page but did not complete payment.
Jackie copied the coach number onto the science sheet, then wrote it again on the corner of an envelope downstairs where somebody searching the recycling might find it.
“If Helen or Brian find that, they’ll tell Mac,” Zoe said.
“And if somebody comes through the house later?”
“Obvious is fine if it looks accidental.”
“That sounds like something from one of your stories.”

Jackie collected stories from the places she had lived after her siblings were separated. Things older children whispered after lights-out. Names adults used only when doors were closed. Rumours about men who found people, erased debts or left rooms full of bodies and no witnesses willing to explain them.
Most of the stories contradicted one another.
“No. That one says never leave evidence. We’re doing the opposite.”
“You threatened a Year Eight with a compass.”

Jackie smiled back, and for several minutes they were simply two girls wasting a Sunday over a ridiculous plan, arguing about whether a ferry terminal had vending machines and whether anybody over the age of thirty understood private messages.
Then footsteps sounded on the landing.
The smiles vanished at the same time.
“Jackie, your hour was over two hours ago.”
The handle moved against the chair.
Jackie swept the papers beneath Zoe’s duvet. Zoe pushed the backpack under the bed. They moved without speaking, each already doing the half of the job the other expected.
When Zoe pulled the chair away, Helen entered carrying two mugs of tea.
She looked from one girl to the other.
Her eyes paused on Jackie’s phone.
“You were told not to contact anyone,” she said to Zoe.
“No,” Jackie replied. “Clever would have been telling people Zoe was missing four days ago.”
Zoe expected anger. Instead Helen placed the mugs on the desk with care, as though the room had tilted and spilling tea would make it worse.
“You don’t know what you’re involved in,” she said.
She had heard versions of that sentence before, from social workers, placement officers and adults who used secrecy as proof of importance.
For one second, there was something in her face that might have become an apology.
“Fine,” Jackie said. “I’ll go to the police station first.”

“Zoe disappeared on Tuesday. School says family emergency. I’ve seen her now. You can either let me stay until she tells me what’s happening, or I explain all of that to somebody who has to write it down.”
“I’ve been asking where she is for five days.”
His expression suggested he had heard enough.
“You are a child in my house.”
“And Zoe is a missing child in your house.”
The optimism adults often mistook for softness had left Jackie’s face completely.
For several seconds, they communicated without speaking.
Keeping Jackie inside and quiet was safer than forcing her into public.
“Until after ten,” Helen said at last. “No calls. No messages. You stay in this room unless we ask you downstairs.”
Jackie switched her phone to flight mode and placed it face up on the desk.
It was the smile she used on teachers when she had already decided which rule she was going to break.
Helen left without taking the phone.
Shortly after four, Brian brought upstairs an envelope containing the itinerary Mac had emailed him to print.
He waited while Zoe opened it.
Inside were a boarding pass, travel instructions and a printed photograph of the man who would meet her after the flight.
His expression in the photograph was neutral, almost tired. Mac had written a number on the back and one sentence beneath it:
He is harmless. Do exactly what he says.
“The car comes at four fifteen tomorrow morning,” he said. “You need to be ready.”
Jackie waited until his steps reached the stairs, then took the papers from Zoe.
Departure before dawn. One direct flight. Arrival early afternoon in another country. A collector waiting beyond customs.
The information made the room feel smaller.
“They won’t expect you to move that early if we make tonight look convincing,” Jackie said.
“Or they’ll expect exactly that because Mac arranged it.”
“Mac knows. The people watching might not.”
“That’s what plans are made of when adults won’t tell you anything.”

The false coach left shortly before midnight. Jackie would leave the house after ten wearing Zoe’s dark coat, hood up, with Zoe’s spare school backpack. They were close enough in height and build for the coat, the darkness and distance to do the rest.
Jackie would walk to the stop on the main road, board the route towards the central coach station and remain visible long enough for anybody watching the house to follow.
The bag would contain old clothes, the copied coach number and a folded route to the ferry terminal.
Jackie would get off two stops before the station, cross through the shopping precinct and call Zoe from the all-night supermarket once she was certain nobody had followed her home.
The spare pay-as-you-go phone would remain with Zoe.
“And if someone does follow you?” Zoe asked.
“I go into the supermarket and call the police.”
“You said the police might not help.”
“I said we can’t assume they know what they’re looking at. A thirteen-year-old being followed by an adult is simple enough even for them.”
Jackie continued folding the route map.
“This isn’t one of your siblings. You don’t have to—”
Zoe wished the sentence back before she had finished saying it.
Jackie looked down at the paper in her hands.
She smoothed the crease with her thumbnail.
“I couldn’t keep them with me,” she said. “That doesn’t mean I stop showing up for people.”

The optimism adults often mistook for softness was gone. Beneath it was the part of Jackie built in kitchens before dawn, in rooms where she listened for her father’s footsteps and decided which child to move first.
“Then you know why I’m not leaving you to do this alone.”
Eventually Zoe said, “No paper with the real route.”
She made Jackie repeat it until every time, location and identifying detail was correct.
The name and photograph of the collector.
The address where he was supposed to take her.
Jackie repeated the details once more without error.
“If I don’t call when I reach the supermarket,” she said, “you assume the decoy failed. You tell Helen the route is exposed and you don’t get in the car.”
“Then scream. Break something. Run to a neighbour. Make it impossible to move you quietly.”
“No. I make it sound like steps. Easy is different.”
They spent the remaining hours trying not to look at the clock.

They ate the biscuits Jackie had brought and watched half an episode of a comedy neither followed. Jackie repaired the broken zip on Zoe’s pencil case with black thread from Helen’s sewing tin. Zoe painted over the bright logo on the spare backpack so it would look more like the one she had carried from school.
At eight, Brian made them come downstairs for dinner.

He served pasta from a jar and watched Jackie too closely. Helen asked about school as though four days of disappearance and a secret international flight could be kept outside the kitchen by discussing a history assignment.
Jackie answered every question with exaggerated politeness.
When Helen asked whether she wanted more food, Jackie said yes and wrapped half of it in a napkin for later without thinking.
Neither mentioned the three children Jackie still fed in her head.
At nine forty-five, they returned upstairs.
Jackie changed into Zoe’s coat. The sleeves were slightly short, but the hood shadowed her face. She put on the spare backpack and turned once in front of the mirror.
“You look like someone trying to steal my identity badly.”
Jackie plugged the spare phone into the wall beside Zoe’s bed.
“Leave it on,” she said. “Don’t message. Don’t call unless I do first.”
“The route is dead. You don’t travel.”
They had always finished each other’s sentences.
That night it felt less like closeness than a way of making sure neither could pretend later that they had misunderstood.
Downstairs, Helen called that it was time.
Jackie opened the bedroom door, then stopped.
She turned back and held out her little finger.
It was something they had done on the first day they met, after Jackie told Zoe that promises made by adults were mostly paperwork and promises made by children needed witnesses.
Zoe hooked her finger around Jackie’s.
Then the brightness returned, deliberate and brave.
Jackie left through the back gate at six minutes past ten.
Zoe watched from the narrow gap between the curtains.
The coat and backpack made Jackie look enough like her at a distance to turn Zoe’s stomach. She walked without hurrying, head down, one hand in the pocket where she had placed the false route.
At the end of the alley, she paused beneath the weak orange light and looked back.
Zoe raised two fingers against the glass.
Then she turned the corner and disappeared.
Zoe remained at the window until the cold from the glass reached her forehead.
The house settled around her. Pipes moved in the walls. Brian checked the back door. Helen carried mugs into the kitchen and left one untouched beside Zoe’s place.
At ten thirty, Zoe sat on the floor with the spare phone in front of her.
At eleven, she told herself the bus was late.
At eleven fifteen, she told herself Jackie was making sure she had not been followed.
At eleven thirty, the phone remained silent.
In the car, Zoe looked down at her hands.
“She was supposed to call,” she said. “That was the whole rule. Whatever happened, she called.”
Elias kept his eyes on the road.
“You didn’t know for certain the house was being watched.”
“I knew it might be. That’s why I sent her out.”
“Because she was the only person you trusted.”
Zoe’s fingers closed around the edge of her sleeve.
“Whoever was watching the house chose what happened after she left. You didn’t.”
“They wouldn’t have had a reason if I hadn’t brought her in.”
Elias was quiet for several seconds.
“Jackie came because you had vanished,” he said. “She stayed because she chose to.”
He left the words where they were. He did not soften them into forgiveness she had not asked for.
The roadworks ended and the traffic dispersed across the open lanes.
“I kept waiting for the phone,” Zoe said. “Even after I knew it wasn’t going to ring.”
Elias glanced at her in the mirror.
Zoe looked towards the backpack at her feet.
“By morning, I had to assume the route was exposed,” she said. “What happened at the other end proved it.”
Elias glanced at her in the mirror, then returned his attention to the motorway.
The late-afternoon light had turned the fields beyond the barrier the colour of old brass. It softened the pylons, service roads and backs of warehouses without improving any of them.
“Take me through the morning,” he said.
Zoe looked down at the backpack between her feet.
At midnight, Jackie still had not called.

Zoe sat on the bedroom floor with the spare phone connected to its charger and the volume turned as high as it would go. The screen dimmed twice. Each time she touched it awake, half expecting the movement to summon the call.
At twelve fifteen, she sent no message.
No calls. No warnings. No second attempt that might reveal where Jackie had gone or who was waiting for her.
The house had become very quiet.

Helen moved once along the landing and stopped outside Zoe’s door. The floorboard gave its usual soft complaint beneath her weight. She remained there long enough for Zoe to see the shadow beneath the gap, then walked away without knocking.
At one, Zoe carried the phone downstairs.
Helen sat at the kitchen table in her cardigan, both hands wrapped around a mug she was not drinking from. Brian stood at the back door with the curtain lifted by one finger.
“She is thirteen,” he said. “Thirteen-year-olds miss calls.”
The words altered the pressure in the room.
Brian looked towards the hallway, as though the sentence might have been heard through the walls.
“We agreed. No call means I don’t travel.”
“Mac arranged this before Jackie came here.”
Helen heard what she had said only after saying it. Her expression changed, but she did not take it back.
Brian crossed the kitchen and removed the phone from Zoe’s hand.
He pulled the charger free, switched the phone off and put it in his pocket.
For one second Zoe considered screaming.
Jackie had told her to make noise. Break something. Run to a neighbour. Make it impossible to move her quietly.
The front door was locked and chained. Brian stood between her and the back door. Helen was already crying, though no tears had fallen yet.
Outside, somebody’s security light came on across the gardens.
A fox moved along the top of a wall and disappeared.
