No pretending she had become wise.
“You do internally.” “Unproven.” Some things survived. Good. They left. Not towards the observation centre. Away.
Cain received the message at ten forty-seven. Restricted legal called him. “Possible P06 exposure.” He stood before the woman finished. “What exposure?” She read the message.
Source authority contradiction. Original presentation site. Thirteen hundred. Cain said nothing. He knew the site. Old Westmere family-assessment centre. Observation rooms. Recipient presentations.
It should have been dead history.
The kind of location nobody revisited because too many things could be reconstructed if they did.
It could mean someone had linked P06 to the site.
An attempt to verify who still reacted.
That last possibility should have slowed him.

“What are you doing?” “Checking.” He ended the call. He knew Jackie’s relocation was expected after the compromised phone. He did not know she was already preparing to leave. Not yet. He picked up his coat.

At ten fifty-eight, Jackie walked out of the house. No hood pulled low. No borrowed identity. No Zoe coat. Her own clothes. A new jacket somebody else had chosen. The legal woman carried a folder. The familiar driver opened the rear door of a dark people carrier. Jackie looked once down the street. Blue recycling bins. Woman with a buggy. White van parked half on the pavement. Nothing dramatic. No Voss. No Vale.

No Elias. Good. Nobody had come for her. She got in. The legal woman sat beside her. The vehicle pulled away. Jackie started counting. Left. Right. Roundabout. Long straight. Lights. Railway crossing. Not because she thought she could build a map from it later. Counting gave fear a job. The legal woman noticed. “You can stop doing that.”
Jackie looked offended. “Maybe I’m counting sheep.”
The woman looked away. Jackie watched the folder instead. Not enough to lean. Not enough to get caught. Two tabs were visible.

She left them alone. Knowing when not to look was useful too. The woman’s phone vibrated. “Yes.” Pause. “No. We’re already mobile.” Another pause. Her expression changed. “That isn’t our route.” Jackie stared through the window. “Who sent it?” Pause. “P06?” Jackie kept her face blank. The woman listened. Then:

“Cain knows?” Pause. “Fine.” She ended the call. The driver checked the mirror. “What?” “Nothing. Stay on route.” Jackie looked outside. Something had happened. She did not know what. Good. That was the point.
At eleven twelve, Voss’s old phone lit.
Vale leaned over. “They answered.” “They responded.” “That is answering.” Voss ignored her. A second message followed.
STANDBY ONLY. DO NOT CONTACT CLIENT.
For once, knowing when to stop felt more professional than knowing how to continue.
At eleven twenty, Vale’s portal changed again.
Closer to the old presentation-site area.
At eleven thirty-eight, Margaret called Mac.
“Old contractor standby appeared. Vehicle reservation changed. Both after a P06 message.”
Cain had turned his attention towards P06.
Someone had introduced uncertainty into different compartments at the same time.
“The first one used a person,” he said.
Only the uncomfortable recognition that the system was now being used against its own habits.
Jackie knew the route had changed because the driver objected.

“Instruction was north.” The legal woman said: “Instruction changed.” “By who?” “Central.” “That isn’t a person.” “Drive.” They left the dual carriageway. More buildings. More traffic. The legal woman made another call. “No, she’s with us.” Pause. “No.” Another pause. “What
site?” Jackie looked at her hands. The woman listened. “That’s unrelated.” Pause. “Fine.” She ended the call. The driver glanced across.

Transfer. So this car had never been the final destination. Jackie filed that away. The move was no longer smooth. People were asking one another questions. That was probably what Zoe wanted. Not a rescue car roaring alongside them. Not Elias appearing with a gun. Hesitation. Jackie almost smiled. The legal woman noticed. “What?”
The woman stared. Jackie smiled properly.

At twelve oh three, they entered the rear yard of a small office building. A solicitor’s plaque faced the street. The legal woman went inside. Jackie stayed in the vehicle with the driver. Five minutes. Seven. Nine. The driver’s phone rang. “Yeah.”
He looked at Jackie in the mirror. “She’s in the vehicle.”
He hung up. Jackie watched the yard. Camera over the gate. One side door.
Maybe he knew what the move really was.
Maybe he knew only that he had been paid to drive a teenager under some kind of restricted case arrangement.
So she did not decide for him.
At twelve thirteen, a separate problem began elsewhere.
Westmere compliance received an internal alert that someone had queried archived access connected to the old presentation centre.
Elaine Foster recognised the site immediately.
Because the centre had already appeared around the restricted cases North Vale was asking about.
She opened the old booking system.
No child names visible in the first layer.
Nobody had told her to preserve them.
That was simply what she did when a current unknown query touched material already under concern.
Another record now existed because somebody had reacted.
At twelve twenty, Elias pulled behind a garden centre.
He switched on the one-use receiver.
VEHICLE RESERVATION SHIFTED TOWARD PRESENTATION SITE.
WESTMERE PRESERVING OLD PRESENTATION-SITE LOGS AFTER
Zoe stared at the screen. “No Jackie.”
“She said she expected to lose the phone.”
Every true sentence made waiting worse. “What if they change everything?”
Zoe looked at him. “That is horrible.”
He did not tell her it would be fine. Good. She reached for the notebook. Stopped. Closed it again. There was nothing useful she could write. Jackie had her piece.
Voss and Vale had stopped after theirs. Now Zoe had to do the part she hated most. Nothing.

At twelve thirty-one, Cain arrived at the old family-assessment centre. One man with him. The reserved Transit arrived a few minutes later. Standby. No Zoe. No Voss. No Vale. No witness waiting by the gate. No secret archive being unloaded. Just a dead building behind fencing. Cain knew before he stepped out of the saloon. Bait. Not necessarily because the message was false. The case number was real. The authority contradiction was real. The site was real. The time had been enough. He had supplied the rest himself. Cain called restricted legal.
Cain looked through the locked gate.
The destination had changed after the phone breach.
The same need-to-know rules that had protected the route for years were now slowing him.
Across the fence, the old centre showed him nothing.
At twelve forty-five, the legal woman returned to Jackie’s vehicle. Angry now. Not panicked. The driver opened his door. “Where?”
Jackie looked at the window. Those words again. The legal woman climbed in. “Take us somewhere public.”
“Public waiting. Services. Station. I don’t care.”
They pulled out. Jackie kept her face neutral. She did not know whether this was good. Good had become a dangerous word.
At twelve fifty-eight, they entered a motorway service area.

Busy. Families. Lorries. Staff in bright uniforms. A school coach two bays away. The legal woman told Jackie: “Stay in the vehicle.” Jackie nodded. The driver and the woman got out and began arguing near the bonnet. Jackie watched them. The rear lock pin was up. Door unlocked. She could open it. Ten feet to the pavement. Twenty to the building. Run inside. Shout. Find security. Call police. Maybe she could get herself out of the car. That did not get her brother and sisters out of anything. It did not tell her whether Cain’s people still knew where they were. It did not tell her who would reach her first after she ran.

And it turned everything after the door into another guess. Jackie stayed seated. The choice hurt more because the door was open. Then she saw the coach. Children in uniform. Teacher counting them. Backpacks. Noise. For half a second her brain offered the old solution. Disappear into them. Confusion. Wrong child. Wrong direction. Zoe’s coat. The first
decoy. No. Jackie stayed where she was. She was not turning another group of children into cover. Not again.
At one oh four, Mac stopped trying to understand the whole picture. He called Margaret. “I need the current duty safeguarding contact.”
“If you make a current disclosure, you do not control what they do next.”
“You may be asked to identify yourself.”
“Cain will know somebody opened the route.”

Margaret gave him the contact. Nothing more. Mac called. He did not give them a command. He could not. He gave them information. A child was currently being moved under disputed authority. There was an active concern about the legitimacy of the transfer. The paperwork chain had produced an authority mismatch. The child had recently been subject to restricted communications. There was reason to believe she had been held across multiple properties. The current movement needed independent safeguarding verification.
The woman on the other end stopped him twice. Asked questions. Some he could answer. Some he could not. Then: “Where is she now?”
Mac gave the service area. “Who is with her?”
He described the legal administrator and vehicle. “Are you the child’s guardian?”
“What is your relationship to this case?”
Mac looked through his office window. There were a dozen answers. None he wanted recorded. “Someone who should have spoken sooner.”
Silence. The woman did not accept that as sufficient. Good.

She asked for his full name. He gave it. Then she told him what would happen. Their decision. Their officers. Their record. Mac would receive no destination afterward. No staff details. No child address. He agreed. Then hung up. For the first time, opening a route meant losing control of it.

The legal woman’s phone rang six minutes later. She answered beside the bonnet. Jackie watched through the window. The woman’s expression changed. Not fear. Calculation. Then irritation. She turned away from the driver. Listened. Argued.
The woman held up one finger.
The woman looked at the vehicle.
“The authority on this transfer is disputed. I’m not moving her again under it.”
Jackie did not know whether the woman had grown a conscience in the last ten minutes.
Maybe she had simply decided she would rather sign a real handover than become the person recorded as moving a child after somebody formally disputed the authority.
Jackie did not care what made the difference.
Two women arrived twenty-one minutes later.
Identification shown to the legal woman first.
The older of the two opened the rear door.
“My name is Sarah. This is Leanne. We’re from the local authority safeguarding team.”
Then stopped when she saw Jackie’s face.
Sarah gave her the public office number.
Nobody told Jackie she was being difficult.
Nobody told her she had to trust them.
When Jackie finally got out of the car, she did it because enough things matched.
Not because somebody opened the door.
The legal woman signed the handover.
Her hand hesitated over the paper.
“Somewhere temporary while we establish what is happening.”
“We need to talk about safe contact first.”
At one seventeen, Zoe’s receiver vibrated.
UNCONFIRMED: CURRENT SAFEGUARDING HANDOVER INITIATED FOR JACKIE. SHADOW TRANSFER APPEARS CANCELLED. DO NOT MOVE.
Zoe went back over the line.
Then a new number appeared through Priya’s relay.
I am in a room with two women who gave me water and asked if I want a solicitor. One has council ID. I asked her to prove it. She laughed. Then proved it.
They can check my brother and sisters through protected contact. They will not tell me where they are unless it is safe. I said okay.
Then got annoyed because she was doing both.
Jackie was communicating from a documented current process with adults who had accepted being challenged.
But out of Cain’s moving chain.
“The decoy didn’t tell them where to take her.”
For somebody else to ask a question.
Enough for the legal woman to refuse another movement.
Enough for a current safeguarding team to arrive.
Zoe understood the difference without writing it down.

At two, Cain learned Jackie had been handed over. Not escaped. That would have been easier. Current authority. Logged. Two local-authority workers. Solicitor offered. The legal administrator had signed the transfer. Cain listened to the report. “Who authorised it?” Nobody answered immediately. He knew what that silence meant. Someone had broken the route. Mac. Margaret. Restricted legal. One of them. Maybe more than one. Cain sat in the saloon outside the observation centre. The standby Transit was still nearby. His people were waiting for instructions.
He had spent years being the person who closed routes. Jackie’s had opened while he was looking somewhere else. He started the engine.

Mac ended his own call and stayed at his desk. The safeguarding team had confirmed receipt of the referral. Nothing more. They would not tell him where Jackie was going. Good. Uncomfortable. Good. Margaret called. “It happened.”
“You understand this does not erase anything.”
Mac looked at the old charity photograph on the shelf. Brian beside him. Years younger. Before Zoe. Before the favour had become a system. “I know.”
“You did one thing.” “Yes.” “Do not confuse it with absolution.” “I’m not.” Margaret was quiet. Then: “Good.” The call ended. Mac turned the photograph face down.

Then agreed to continue. Annoying. Functional. Her phone remained quiet until five ten. Then Jackie appeared through Priya’s protected relay. Siblings checked. All alive. They won’t tell me where. I said okay. Another message: I hate saying okay.
I told them about Cain. Houses. Legal woman. Phones. Moves. Anything I actually know.
Not your current location because I do not know it.
Tell her I finally have one useful secret.
Then, because some things deserved to remain stupid:
And for that evening, that was enough.
Saturday morning, Jackie said no three times before breakfast.
No, she did not want the door left open.
No, she did not want the officer from yesterday sitting in.
No, she did not want anyone contacting her siblings yet.
The solicitor wrote all three down.
The room was in a council building that looked exactly like every council building Jackie had ever imagined.
A clock that made too much noise.
A box of tissues positioned where someone had decided frightened people would see it.
The solicitor was called Nisha Patel.
Office number called independently from a council phone.
Nisha had tolerated the whole process with suspicious good humour.
She did not let it change anything.
Across the table sat Claire, the safeguarding officer who had collected most of Jackie’s first account the night before.

Claire almost smiled. Jackie caught her.

Elias knew because she had not complained about the curtains.
Their room sat above a pub in a village where apparently nobody believed Saturday morning should begin before ten.
He sat by the window with coffee.

Her hair pointed in several directions at once.
Inside a process Zoe did not control.
For once, that was not automatically a bad thing.

The fourth was the suburban house. Some adults appeared at more than one place. Same legal woman twice. Same driver three times. Cain twice. Another man Jackie never identified appeared at three. Claire asked: “What made you think Cain was in charge?”

Claire stopped. Jackie noticed. Adults liked simple shapes.

Margaret Shaw sat opposite him in a hotel lounge twenty miles from his house.
She had refused every location connected to him.
“That you referred a child into current safeguarding after discovering her transfer authority was disputed.”

He looked at the time. Then at the message. “No.”

Margaret leaned forward. “You are still talking as though Cain is the only problem.”
She held his gaze. “He is not the only record of what you did.”

The request reached Zoe before noon.
Current safeguarding wanted Zoe offered independent legal advice.
The solicitor would be Zoe’s choice.

The purpose was to establish that she was alive, could speak for herself and had wishes of her own.
“Voice. Metadata. Whatever legal duties the solicitor has.”

Zoe looked down at the message.
One had connections she did not want to untangle.
Another was unsuitable for the remote setup they needed.
No obvious connection to Westmere, Meridian, North Vale, Voss, Mac or anybody else already inside the story.
Elias called the published office number.
Then looked at Ruth Ellison’s name again. “I’ll speak to her.” No permission asked. None given.

Silence. Cain heard it. He changed direction. “Did you know Jackie had been handed into current safeguarding?”

The voice on the other end was steady now.
Someone had simply stopped obeying him.

It came from the safeguarding review opened after North Vale and Westmere compared historic records.
Whether anyone had instructed them not to speak directly to statutory authorities.
Whether they believed Zoe was currently missing or at risk.
Helen read the final question twice.
Brian sat at the kitchen table.
He stopped himself. Helen stared. “Stupid,” Brian said.
He almost smiled. Didn’t. Helen opened the letter again. “They know enough to ask.”
Brian rubbed his hands together. “We could say we thought it was private adoption.”
Silence. “We could say Mac handled the legal side.”
Brian stared at the table. Helen waited.
The word sat between them. Five years late.
At two, Jackie asked to stop.
“And I’m not eating sandwiches from that fridge.”
The room became something else for a few minutes.
Jackie bought chips from the café downstairs.
Nisha sat opposite her. “You know you don’t have to solve Zoe’s case.”
Jackie looked up. Everyone had started doing that. Annoying. “I have information.”
Jackie frowned at the chips. “I spent my whole life doing things for other people.”

Nisha did not rush to fix that. “You don’t have to learn today.”
That answer irritated her less than most.

The clause that allowed private placement-support referrals through restricted legal channels.
Nothing about where Zoe was now.
“If I disappear, somebody should have the part with my name on it.”

Mac looked through the windscreen of the car he had parked at a motorway services.
Had not decided where he would sleep.
“When her own representative considers it relevant and safe.”
At three fifteen, Cain tried to find Jackie.
Not through the people who had moved her.
There was now a safeguarding record.
One old contact could establish that much.
He simply did not have the right to open it.
For years, that distinction had been something people around him could bend.
Cain stared at the access denial.
Zoe answered from a prepaid handset.
“Before you tell me anything, I need to explain who I am and who I am not.”

“I also cannot promise absolute confidentiality in every circumstance. If you tell me somebody is in immediate danger, there may be situations where I have to act.”
When she did not know, she said:
Dangerous. “Do you want to continue?” Ruth asked.
Zoe paused. Not because Ruth did not know it. Because saying it herself mattered. “Zoe.”
“Thank you. Do you know where you are?”
Nothing else. No push. “Are you being prevented from leaving?”
“Has anyone threatened you if you leave?”
“Has he told you what to say to me?”
He walked out and closed the door.
“Are you travelling with Elias because you choose to be?”
“Do you believe you would be safer if statutory services knew your current location?”
Zoe looked at the backpack beside the bed.
“The people who took me had access to systems that were supposed to protect children. I don’t know which parts are safe yet.”
Ruth was quiet for a moment.
Not what evidence do you have.
Zoe looked at the closed door.
“I want people to stop making decisions about my information without me.”
“And her brother and sisters. But nobody uses them to get to her.”
“There are other children in the records I have. They didn’t choose any of this.”
“I want the adults who did it investigated.”
“But I don’t want every foster carer or social worker dragged into it because somebody used something legitimate around them.”
“And Helen and Brian don’t decide what happens to me next.”
“Who are Helen and Brian to you?”
“My preliminary view is that your wishes need to exist independently in the record before other people start making decisions around you.”
“Nothing. I just suspect you prefer adults who admit when an answer might change.”
The call lasted almost an hour.
When Elias came back, Zoe was sitting on the floor with her back against the bed.
He did not ask what she had said.
“My wishes are in somebody else’s file now.”
At five thirty, Helen and Brian called an independent family-law solicitor.
Helen told the receptionist they needed advice about a historic placement that might not have been lawful.
Helen put her hand over his.
The solicitor asked whether a child was currently at risk.
“We reported it through someone we trusted.”
This was the first real threshold.
At six twelve, Margaret sent Mac’s agreement to Priya and to independent counsel involved in the safeguarding review.
The document now existed somewhere Mac could not quietly retrieve every version of it.

At seven, Claire showed Jackie a temporary placement option. Not the address yet. A description. Small staff team. No other children currently living there. Independent advocacy available. Restricted records. Jackie read the page. “Can I say no?”
The place sounded boring. Excellent. “Can I see it before deciding?”
Nobody had stood behind glass deciding whether Jackie fit.
Nobody had already accepted on her behalf.
At seven forty, Priya called Voss.
Priya did not ask for another reconstruction.
She already had enough of those.
“If what you’ve both told me is going to be useful,” she said, “it needs to stop being an informal account.”
“Statements. Signed. Limited to what each of you personally saw, did, retained or can actually support.”
Later, Zoe and Elias ate takeaway in the room above the pub.
Elias had something in a cardboard box that she had stopped asking questions about.
The receiver stayed off during food.
Somewhere else, Jackie had been offered a place and had not accepted it.
Helen and Brian had finally said Mac’s name to somebody who did not work for him.
Cain had found a file he could see but could not open.
And tomorrow Voss and Vale would put their own names beneath what they had done.
“What?” “Nothing.” “Suspicious.” “Normal.” He went back to his food. Zoe smiled. For once, she let the day end without explaining it.
Sunday morning, Voss signed his name.
Not because the signature looked wrong.
The same signature he had put on invoices, vehicle leases, contractor agreements, expense claims and Christmas cards he never wanted to write.

Now it sat beneath seventeen pages explaining how his team had moved a child from a legitimate temporary placement into a private receiving household using authority that the issuing institution said it had never created.
Priya Dey sat across the table.
Three copies of the contractor statement lay in front of her.
One for independent counsel working with the institutional review.
One sealed for Voss and Vale.
The yellow-coat case existed only as a historic identifier and a sequence of actions they could personally support.
Priya turned to the declaration page.
“Before I witness these, I need to ask you both again. Are you signing voluntarily?”
“Have I promised either of you immunity?”
“Have I told you this guarantees favourable treatment?”
“Have either of you been offered something in return?”
“Legacy counsel offered a favourable characterisation if we surrendered retained material.”
“Because I stopped trusting the people offering it.”
She ignored him. “I didn’t want them writing it for me.”
Priya waited. Vale looked at the statement beneath her signature. “I was there.”
“I want my part to say what I did.”
Priya wrote that on her interview pad. Separate from the statement. Then she witnessed both signatures. No forgiveness. No deal. Just their names beneath their own account.

At nine twenty, Zoe spoke to Ruth Ellison. Elias was already outside the room. Zoe had asked him to leave before Ruth had even mentioned it. Ruth noticed. Didn’t comment. Good. “I’ve received some adult-side records that may relate to you,” she said. “What records?”
“Voss and Vale’s signed statements. A sponsor agreement supplied through separate counsel. And confirmation that North Vale and Westmere are preserving a restricted group of historic cases.”
“North Vale and Westmere now have records of their own. Priya has the contractor statements. Mac’s agreement exists independently of your copy.”
Zoe rubbed her thumb against the side of the chair.
The backpack was beside the bed. The drive inside it. Still important. No longer alone. “Don’t put everything together yet.”
“I don’t want one person holding the only complete version.”
“That may change once investigators require material.”
“But for now, the sources can remain separately preserved.”
Ruth paused. “I also need to tell you something about Helen and Brian.”
That landed harder than Zoe expected.
“Their solicitor contacted the safeguarding review. They have agreed to separate voluntary interviews.”
“To protect the independence of what they remember.”
Zoe looked towards the closed door.
“If it becomes relevant to your legal position and disclosure is appropriate.”
Helen and Brian sat in separate rooms.
That word had been explained carefully.

Three days later, Zoe changed her mind. Partly. “First page.” Ruth placed Helen’s envelope on the table. “Only the first?” “Yes.” “Okay.” Zoe pointed at her. “Careful.”
The first sentence filled almost two lines.
I am not going to begin by telling you how much I love you, because you asked me not to make this about that.
I knew enough to say no. I said yes instead.

I cannot make the choice smaller by telling you what I was grieving, what I had lost, or what I believed I could give you. Those things explain me. They do not give me the right to have chosen for you or for the family you came from.
The protected accommodation came through current safeguarding.
Ruth had made sure Zoe understood who could know the location and why. Claire had explained the practical rules. None of them pretended the arrangement was permanent.
Elias had a separate room down the corridor.
The first time Zoe slept in the same building two nights in a row, she woke at three in the morning convinced she had forgotten something.
She got dressed and went downstairs.

Not exactly. But nothing was attacking her either. She sat by the window. At three seventeen, the lift opened. Elias came out wearing a T-shirt and shoes without socks. Zoe looked him up and down. “You sensed a disturbance in the force?”
He sat opposite. Did not ask what was wrong. After a while Zoe said: “What if normal feels wrong forever?”
She looked at him. “You don’t know that.”
He rubbed his face. “It may for a while.”
Better. Zoe pulled her sleeves over her hands.
“Jackie says the boring house is too quiet.”
That was how she found out.
The doctor knew about the rib pain.
Part of the pain plan changed.
He also took what he had been prescribed instead of trying to prove something by refusing it.
She had enough people to manage.
Two weeks after Daniel’s article, Ruth asked: “What name do you want used in the proceedings?”
The earlier name in the folder.
The identity assigned after everything changed.
“Some records may need correcting eventually. You do not have to settle every part of that today.”
“Even if somebody else chose it first?”
“What if I want to know the other name too?”
“What if I don’t want to pick one and throw the other away?”
Knowing where she came from did not mean she had to become a stranger overnight.
Keeping Zoe did not mean Helen and Brian still owned the decision.
An adult recording what Zoe wanted.

A teacher asked the class to write about resilience. Jackie refused on principle. The teacher gave her coastal erosion instead. Jackie considered this proof that institutions were capable of learning. Zoe laughed so hard she had to hang up and call back. Zoe’s own schooling restarted more slowly. Tutor first. Maths. English. Science. She discovered that surviving a conspiracy did not improve algebra. Deeply unfair.

The article stopped being front-page news. Faster than Zoe expected. Other things happened. The world continued. The investigations did too. Westmere’s review widened. Other authorities checked old restricted records against original legal files. Some came back clean. Some did not. Some remained uncertain.
No magical number appeared to explain everything.
Nobody honest claimed the job was finished.
Best decision she had made all month.
One afternoon, she and Jackie sat on a bench beside the park.
A dog was attempting to drag a stick through railings despite the stick being wider than the gap.
It had failed several times and remained committed.
“I thought getting away would feel bigger.”
Zoe watched the dog abandon the stick and run off after something else.
“You can get out of a room and still have everyone deciding what happens next.”
Ruth asking what she wanted. Jackie saying no. A bathroom lock. A sealed letter. A name she did not have to surrender. A drive she no longer carried. “Agency.”
Jackie made a face. “That sounds like homework.”
Zoe smiled. The opposite of captivity was agency. They watched the dog come back without the stick.
Elias packed on a Thursday. Zoe knew before he told her. His bag sat on the chair.
Not much inside. Elias had never owned enough for dramatic packing. She stood in the doorway. “Where are you going?”
He looked up. “Need to sort a few things.”
He zipped the bag. “The immediate threat has changed.”
Elias looked at her. “You don’t need me in the same way.”
Zoe stared at him. “That wasn’t the question.”
She stepped into the room. “You keep deciding that leaving is safer for everyone else.”
Silence. No evidence. No plan. Nothing Zoe could prove. Elias said: “Zoe.”
He stopped. “You don’t get to decide for me that I’m better without you.”
“It is when you’re making my decision as well.”
Elias sat on the edge of the bed. His bag remained beside him. Zoe said: “If you want to leave, say you want to leave.”
He looked at her. “If you’re tired of this, say that.”
Nothing. “But don’t turn leaving into something you’re doing for me.”
The room went quiet. Zoe waited. He could still go. That had to remain true. Finally Elias said: “I don’t know how to stay without becoming responsible for everything.”
Her anger changed shape. She sat in the chair opposite him. “Then don’t.”
“There will be decisions I have to make.”
Zoe leaned back. “Simple answers are suspicious.”
That almost got a laugh. Almost. She looked at his bag. “Do you want to leave?”
Something in Zoe’s chest hurt in a way she did not entirely dislike. “Then unpack.”
He looked at her. “Bossy.” “Agency.” “That is not what agency means.” “It does today.” Elias laughed. Actually laughed. Then opened the bag. He took out a shirt. Then another. Not everything. Enough.

Saturday morning, the cheap phone buzzed while Zoe was eating toast. She looked at the screen. Ruth. A short update. Cain’s next hearing date. Another historic authority reference confirmed for formal review. Nothing requiring Zoe that day. Zoe read it once. Turned the phone off. Elias watched from across the table.

“No reply?” “Nothing to say.” She dropped it into the backpack beside the fantasy book. The bag contained water. Crisps. The book. A switched-off phone. Nothing anyone would kill for. “Walk?” Elias asked. Zoe looked out of the window. “Why?” He shrugged. “Because.” Suspicious. Acceptable.

The path outside town followed a hedge for nearly a mile before splitting. Left climbed towards a ridge. Right dropped towards a river. A wooden sign gave distances Zoe had not bothered memorising. Elias stopped at the junction. Zoe stopped beside him. The backpack hung loose from one shoulder.
Zoe looked at the ridge. Then at the river. “What do you think?”
Elias glanced at her. Then towards the paths. “River.”
Zoe looked towards the river. Then back at the ridge. “I want the view.”
He looked at both paths again. “Ridge first. River on the way back.” Zoe considered. “Acceptable.” They turned left.
